title: When does an IPO count?
hook: A filing, a plan and a completed listing are different events.
headline: Will Company A go public before Company B?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires Company A's shares to begin regular trading on a public exchange before Company B's shares do, and before the stated deadline. A confidential filing, public filing or announcement of intent does not count as the first trading day.
plainRule: Company A's first regular trading day must happen before Company B's and before the deadline.
trap: A headline about an IPO filing can arrive months before a listing. The order of actual trading days decides this example.

scenarios.question: Company A files its IPO papers first, but no shares trade yet. Is YES established?
scenarios.why: The sample rule requires the first regular trading day, not a filing.

scenarios.question: Company A starts regular trading before Company B and before the deadline. Does that meet YES?
scenarios.why: All three explicit conditions in the sample rule are met.

scenarios.question: Both companies begin trading on the same date, with no time-order rule. Can this example decide the winner?
scenarios.why: A tie rule would be needed to decide same-day starts.

title: Does one hot month count?
hook: A monthly spike cannot satisfy an annual test.
headline: Will global warming cross the threshold?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires an annual global temperature average to exceed the specified baseline by at least 2.0°C in a calendar year before the deadline. Two independent named agencies must publish qualifying annual results.
plainRule: A qualifying annual result and two independent agency reports are both required.
trap: The period and number of sources matter. A monthly record or one early estimate leaves the condition unfinished.

scenarios.question: One month exceeds the threshold but the annual average does not. Does it count?
scenarios.why: The sample rule measures a full calendar year.

scenarios.question: A qualifying annual average is published by two named agencies before the deadline. Does it meet YES?
scenarios.why: The period, threshold, source count and deadline all match the sample rule.

scenarios.question: One agency has reported; the second has not yet published. Is the final result known?
scenarios.why: The second required report may still arrive.

title: Which milestone happens first?
hook: A test run does not necessarily start a public service.
headline: Will a human land on Mars before a new rail service opens?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires the first confirmed human landing on Mars to occur before the first ticketed passenger service on a specified high-speed rail line, with both milestones compared in UTC. An uncrewed landing and a rail test run do not qualify.
plainRule: Compare a human landing with the first ticketed passenger service, using their verified UTC timestamps.
trap: Two newsworthy previews may happen before either contract milestone. Only the qualifying events enter the ordering test.

scenarios.question: An uncrewed spacecraft lands on Mars first. Does it satisfy YES?
scenarios.why: The sample rule requires a human landing.

scenarios.question: A human lands before the first ticketed passenger trip. Does that meet YES?
scenarios.why: The qualifying Mars milestone happened first.

scenarios.question: A rail test run happens, but no passenger service or human Mars landing follows yet. Is the result known?
scenarios.why: Neither qualifying milestone has occurred.

title: Which deadline actually applies?
hook: “Before the earlier of” creates a moving cutoff.
headline: Will the explorer visit Mars in their lifetime?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires the named explorer to personally visit Mars before the earlier of their death or 1 January 2100, 00:00 UTC. Sending equipment, robots or representatives does not qualify.
plainRule: The personal visit must precede both the person's death and the fixed cutoff.
trap: A lifetime headline can hide a fixed outer deadline. The earliest applicable endpoint controls.

scenarios.question: The explorer personally visits before 2100 while alive. Does that meet YES?
scenarios.why: The personal visit is before both endpoints.

scenarios.question: A robot named after the explorer reaches Mars. Does that count?
scenarios.why: The sample rule requires the person to visit.

scenarios.question: The explorer visits after the fixed 2100 cutoff while still alive. Does it meet YES?
scenarios.why: The fixed cutoff has already passed.

title: When is a base a colony?
hook: Headcount and duration are separate conditions.
headline: Will humans colonize Mars by the deadline?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires at least ten people to reside continuously in a self-sufficient settlement on Mars for one full Earth year, with that year completed before the deadline. Self-sufficiency means no essential food, air or water shipments from Earth during that year.
plainRule: Ten residents, a full Earth year and no essential resupply must coincide before the cutoff.
trap: A landing, short stay or regularly resupplied base is not the specified one-year colony.

scenarios.question: Ten people live there for six months. Does that satisfy YES?
scenarios.why: The continuous year has not finished.

scenarios.question: Twelve residents complete a year without essential Earth shipments before the deadline. Does it meet YES?
scenarios.why: The headcount, duration and supply conditions are all met.

scenarios.question: Ten people complete a year, but shipment records are unavailable. Is YES established?
scenarios.why: The self-sufficiency condition cannot yet be verified.

title: When does a proof count?
hook: A preprint and a recognized result have different status.
headline: Will the conjecture be solved this year?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires a complete proof or counterexample to be published in a named peer-reviewed journal before the deadline and not formally retracted before resolution. A preprint or social post alone is insufficient.
plainRule: The result needs named peer-reviewed publication before the cutoff and must survive the retraction window.
trap: The first exciting manuscript may be followed by review, correction or withdrawal.

scenarios.question: A viral preprint claims a proof. Is YES established?
scenarios.why: The named peer-reviewed publication has not happened.

scenarios.question: A qualifying journal publishes the proof before the deadline, and it is not retracted before resolution. Does it meet YES?
scenarios.why: The publication and retraction conditions both hold.

scenarios.question: A qualifying article appears, but a formal retraction review is pending. Is the final result certain?
scenarios.why: The retraction window has not closed.

title: Can YES pay less than one?
hook: A tie clause can split the payout.
headline: Which discovery happens first?
rule: In this fictional contract, a named discovery pays 1/N if it shares the first verified timestamp with N qualifying discoveries. It pays 1 if it is uniquely first, and 0 if another qualifying discovery is first. Verification follows the same named source for every discovery.
plainRule: The payout can be 1, 1/N or 0 depending on verified ordering and ties.
trap: A binary-looking headline does not guarantee a binary payout when a tie clause is present.

scenarios.question: The named discovery is uniquely first. Does one unit pay 1?
scenarios.why: The sample rule gives a full payout to the unique first discovery.

scenarios.question: Three qualifying discoveries share the first timestamp. Does this unit pay 1?
scenarios.why: It pays 1/3 under the explicit tie clause.

scenarios.question: Two sources publish different timestamps and no source hierarchy is stated. Can the payout be calculated?
scenarios.why: A source hierarchy or verified timestamp is needed.

title: Which Bitcoin price counts?
hook: A dashboard tick is not always the settlement print.
headline: Will BTC close above the target?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires the BTC/USD reference rate published by Index A at 23:59 UTC on the deadline date to be strictly greater than $100,000. An exchange spot price, a chart preview and an equal reading do not qualify.
plainRule: Use Index A's exact deadline print and a strict greater-than comparison.
trap: Different feeds can disagree. The named settlement source and equality boundary control this example.

scenarios.question: A popular exchange shows $100,200, but Index A prints $99,900 at the deadline. Does YES hold?
scenarios.why: The sample rule names Index A as the source.

scenarios.question: Index A prints $100,001 at the exact deadline. Does YES hold?
scenarios.why: The named print is strictly greater than the threshold.

scenarios.question: Index A has not published the deadline print yet. Is the outcome known?
scenarios.why: The required source value is missing.

title: Can a ceasefire still finish in time?
hook: A continuous streak has a last possible start.
headline: Will a ceasefire last 14 days before month-end?
rule: In this fictional contract, YES requires fourteen uninterrupted 24-hour periods without a qualifying hostile action. The full streak must end by 31 December at 23:59 UTC. Any qualifying hostile action resets the count to zero at its verified timestamp.
plainRule: Fourteen full days must finish by the cutoff, with no qualifying reset event.
trap: A declaration of peace cannot substitute for elapsed time. Use the deadline clock to find the latest possible start.

scenarios.question: A ceasefire is announced five days before the cutoff. Can a new 14-day streak finish in time?
scenarios.why: Only five days remain; the required 14-day duration cannot fit.

scenarios.question: A streak starts at least 14 days before the cutoff and no qualifying action occurs. Does it meet YES?
scenarios.why: The full continuous period fits inside the window.

scenarios.question: A disputed incident occurs during the streak. Can the page decide whether it resets the clock?
scenarios.why: The incident must be checked against the contract's qualifying-action definition and source.

title: What counts as a breakthrough?
hook: Undefined milestone words need a decision rule.
headline: Will fusion be achieved before the deadline?
rule: This fictional draft says only: ‘YES if practical nuclear fusion is achieved before 1 January 2030.’ It does not define practical, name a measurement, or identify an authoritative source. The examples below show why this draft is not ready to resolve reliably.
plainRule: The draft lacks an operational definition of practical fusion and a deciding source.
trap: A precise date cannot rescue an undefined event. This is a drafting problem to fix before anyone relies on the contract.

scenarios.question: A lab announces a record fusion experiment. Is YES established by this draft?
scenarios.why: The draft never defines ‘practical’ or a qualifying measurement.

scenarios.question: A commercial reactor is announced but not operating. Is YES established?
scenarios.why: The draft does not say whether an announcement, demonstration or operation qualifies.

scenarios.question: The event happens after the fixed deadline. Can it satisfy YES?
scenarios.why: The only unambiguous condition in the draft is the deadline.
